q: A kettle transforms $120\,000\,\text{J}$ of electrical energy in $60\,\text{s}$. What is its power?
What is $1\,\text{kWh}$ in joules, and is the kilowatt-hour a unit of power or of energy?
a: $1\,\text{kWh} = 1000\,\text{W} \cdot 3600\,\text{s} = 3\,600\,000\,\text{J}$. The kilowatt-hour is a unit of energy, because it is power (kW) times time (h).

q: Why can a $5.0\,\text{W}$ standby consume more energy in a year than a $2000\,\text{W}$ kettle used for $3.0\,\text{min}$ a day?
a: Energy is power times time. Standby is on for $8760\,\text{h}$ a year and consumes (substituting $1\,\text{W} = 10^{-3}\,\text{kW}$, so $5.0\,\text{W} = 5.0 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\text{kW} = 0.0050\,\text{kW}$) $0.0050\,\text{kW} \cdot 8760\,\text{h} = 43.8\,\text{kWh} \approx 44\,\text{kWh}$. The kettle is on for $3.0\,\text{min} \cdot 365 = 1095\,\text{min}$. Substituting $1\,\text{min} = 1\,\text{h} : 60$, we get $1095\,\text{min} = 1095 \cdot (1\,\text{h} : 60) = 18.25\,\text{h}$, and it consumes $2.0\,\text{kW} \cdot 18.25\,\text{h} = 36.5\,\text{kWh} \approx 37\,\text{kWh}$. The results are rounded to two significant figures like the given values. A low power for a long time beats a high power for a short time.
